title: The second arrow
hook: the first arrow is pain; the second is our reaction to it (Samyutta Nikaya 36.6)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the first truth, a plain list, and your line was name it first. Did something go wrong that you gave a plain name before you fixed it? Today, what happens right after the naming. Day seven hundred one.

A dark kitchen, a glass of water, no lights on. A bare foot meets the leg of a chair, hard. That's the first part, and it's sharp, and it's real. Then the second part arrives, about half a second later. Who moved this chair. Why does this always happen to me. I can't even get a glass of water. Now the toe hurts, and so does the whole night. Often, what keeps us awake is the second part. A short teaching of the Buddha has a name for each of them. It calls them arrows.
screen: `A BARE FOOT, A CHAIR LEG.` → `THEN, HALF A SECOND LATER…` → `TWO ARROWS.`

segments.voice: First, same pain, two people. In the Samyutta Nikaya there's a teaching called the Arrow. The Buddha says that an untaught person and a trained disciple both feel things: pleasant, painful and neither. Pain comes to both. The difference is what happens next. When the untaught person is touched by pain, the text says, he sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast and becomes distraught. Second, one arrow, then another. It's like this, the Buddha says. A man is struck by an arrow, and then struck by a second arrow right after it. Now he feels the pain of two. The first is the pain in the body. The second is the pain the mind adds: the sorrowing, the lamenting, the beating of the breast. Third, some second arrows look like comfort. Then the text adds something. It says that the untaught person, touched by pain, goes looking for sense pleasure, because he knows no other way out of pain. So a second arrow isn't always a rant. Sometimes it's the snack, the scroll, the drink, reached for so that the first arrow doesn't have to be felt. Fourth, the first one still hurts. The trained disciple, the Buddha says, feels the first arrow and not the second. Bodily pain, yes. The added layer, no. This isn't a promise of numbness. The toe still throbs. The body still hurts. What drops away is the extra wound we fire into ourselves. This arrow, by the way, isn't the poisoned arrow from the parable we heard back in year one. Different teaching, same honesty about pain.
screen: `SAME PAIN, TWO PEOPLE.` · `ONE ARROW, THEN ANOTHER.` · `SOME SECOND ARROWS LOOK LIKE COMFORT.` · `THE FIRST ONE STILL HURTS.` · then, large: `SKIP THE SECOND ARROW.`

segments.voice: Sit, and wait for something slightly uncomfortable to show up. It will: an itch, a stiff shoulder, a sound you don't like, a worry drifting in. When it comes, find the first arrow. Just the plain sensation. Then watch for the second, the commentary that arrives right behind it: ugh, not this, why now. You don't have to stop it. Just notice it as a second arrow, and come back to the first one, which may be smaller than it seemed. Do this as many times as it comes. The bell holds the time.
The second arrow: in the Buddha's teaching, the pain the mind adds to the pain that comes. The first arrow is felt; the second is fired by us. Today's word.
Your line: skip the second arrow. Today, when something stings, catch one second arrow as it flies, the rant or the reach for comfort, and let the first arrow be enough. Day seven hundred one.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the two arrows to describe how the mind adds suffering to pain, and meditators practice noticing bodily sensation directly while letting the added commentary pass.

fork.setup: you're the trained disciple in the Buddha's teaching. pain arrives in your body. what happens?
options: you feel the bodily pain, but not the added sorrow
you feel the pain of two arrows
fork.reveal: one arrow, not two: the disciple feels bodily pain without the second, mental wound.

original.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: feeling, pleasant, painful or neither, the word the arrow teaching is built on.

trapdoor: what you thought: a calm person doesn't feel pain.
what it means: everyone is hit by the first arrow; the trained mind stops firing the second into itself.
what a scholar hears: Samyutta Nikaya 36.6, the Sallatha Sutta, where the untaught person feels two feelings, bodily and mental, and the instructed disciple feels only the bodily one.

notes: Editor: hook moved off 'two in the morning' (day 694 opened at three in the morning); stock line 'here's the part that's easy to miss' cut; 'the loss still aches' replaced, since in the sutta the disciple feels only the bodily feeling, and grief over a loss is the mental one.

SN 36.6 paraphrased throughout: the uninstructed worldling and the instructed noble disciple both feel the three kinds of feeling; the worldling, touched by painful feeling, sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast, becomes distraught, and feels two feelings, bodily and mental, like a man struck by a second arrow.
The sutta also says the worldling, touched by pain, seeks delight in sensual pleasure because he knows no escape from pain other than sensual pleasure. Confirm this is fairly summarized.
The modern examples of the second arrow (snack, scroll, drink) are the script's own, not the sutta's.
Original: Pali vedanā in Devanagari (वेदना); confirm.
